Noir fiction, a genre characterized by its dark, moody atmosphere and morally complex characters, has a rich history that spans several decades and continents. Pioneered by American writers like Elliott Chaze, Charles Williams, Gil Brewer, Harry Whittington, Peter Rabe, and Lionel White, along with David Goodis and Jim Thompson, this literary trend has continued to develop and grow throughout the years. In the 1980s, Black Lizard, an American publisher, played a significant role in reviving interest in noir fiction by re-releasing many classic works. Today, Akashic Books continues to celebrate the genre with a diverse collection of noir short-story anthologies. The noir genre has also gained significant traction in Europe, featuring prominent writers like Jean-Claude Izzo and Massimo Carlotto who have played a key role in its development. According to Italian publisher Sandro Ferri, "Mediterranean noir" stands out for its exploration of the dual nature of Mediterranean life. These novels often depict Mediterranean cities as places that have been marred by crime, yet still possess a captivating charm. The genre is characterized by a dual perspective, contrasting the Mediterranean way of life, which values good wine, great food, strong friendships, and lively social gatherings, with the darker aspects of violence, corruption, greed, and misuse of power. Among contemporary authors who blend elements of hardboiled and noir styles, James Ellroy emerges as a central figure. He defines noir as "the most intensely examined branch of the hard-boiled tradition," and emphasizes its attraction through the "thrill of moral compromise and the surrender to sensation." Ellroy also acknowledges the social significance of noir, highlighting its examination of critical issues such as race, class, gender, and systemic challenges. Noir fiction's enduring popularity can be attributed to its ability to delve into the complexities of human nature and society, offering readers a compelling and thought-provoking experience.

The concept of having no opinion, known as [Greek: epochê], is a state that leads to a sense of tranquility called [Greek: ataraxia]. Pyrrho, a philosopher whose questions were posed in a manner reminiscent of Kant, sought not to develop a system of truth but to explore the nature of philosophy itself. His dedication to this pursuit is illustrated by an anecdote from Diogenes, in which Pyrrho was found talking to himself, contemplating how to become a virtuous person ([Greek: chrêstos]). This story reveals a depth of character distinct from the typical skepticism found in Sextus' works. The core of Pyrrho's philosophy and his way of living can primarily be traced back to his individual temperament. His indifference was inherent to his calm nature and was not solely a product of his philosophical beliefs. While this attitude could be aspired to, it could never be fully replicated. One of his followers pointed out that to genuinely adopt Pyrrho's teachings, an individual would need to exhibit the same way of thinking. Diogenes records that Pyrrho was the first to propose the rudimentary principles of skepticism, although his ideas were not yet fully developed, as he left no written works. There is no evidence of Pyrrho formulating the Tropes, but it is likely that he recognized some contradictions in sensory experiences, possibly hinting at the Tropes in a nascent form. Among the many skeptical maxims, or [Greek: phônai], the three that are most closely associated with the origins of skepticism are the [Greek: antilogia], the [Greek: ouden horizô], and the [Greek: ou mallon]. Diogenes cites Protagoras as the source for the idea that there are always two opposing arguments for everything. The phrase "to determine nothing" is attributed to Timon's _Python_, and the other two maxims are also linked to him by Aristocles. The [Greek: ou mallon] has a direct connection with Democritus, although the interpretation of this phrase by Pyrrho was likely different, as indicated by Sextus. It is probable that Pyrrho employed all three of these sayings, as suggested by Diogenes. However, this led to accusations from the Dogmatics that the Skeptics were dogmatizing simply by possessing such sayings. Sextus countered this claim by asserting that these maxims also contain their own inherent meaning, much like how a purgative eliminates itself alongside other toxic elements. In comparing the later Pyrrhonism with the teachings of Pyrrho, there is a stark contrast in the moral stance of the two. For Pyrrho, the equilibrium of the soul was a means to apply to his positive theory of life, whereas for the later Pyrrhoneans, it was the ultimate goal. However, the empirical tendency that characterized the history of Pyrrhonism can be traced back to Pyrrho as its originator. He was an empiricist thinker, and his impact in this area stood in sharp contrast to the dialectical approach of Academic Skepticism. The empiricism of the school is evident in its scientific knowledge, the fact that many Skeptics were physicians, and in the nature of the ten Tropes of [Greek: epochê]. It is reasonable to claim that the core tenets of Pyrrhonism can be traced back to Pyrrho and his innovative ideas, which provided the school with its essential foundation. However, the more elaborate arguments and the specifics of its maxims belong to later periods. Regarding the relationship between Pyrrhonism and the Academy, the connection is challenging to pinpoint with precision, especially between the time of Pyrrho and Aenesidemus. However, skepticism within the Academy was never entirely the same as Pyrrhonism, even though there were periods in the history of the Academy when the difference was minimal. Arcesilaus, who introduced doubt into the Academy, aimed to return to the dialectic of Socrates. He replaced lectures with discussions, which he believed to be a more Socratic method of teaching. Despite Sextus' assertion that Arcesilaus' skepticism was the closest to Pyrrhonism, his teachings were fundamentally rooted in the dialectical principle, which was in opposition to the empiricism of Pyrrho. The belief in the existence of absolute truth, as held by Socrates and Plato, never completely lost its influence over the Academy. This belief eventually led the Academy back to Dogmatism and paved the way for the Eclecticism that marked its departure from history. The histories of Pyrrhonism and Academic Skepticism were contemporaneous for some time. Timon, the immediate follower of Pyrrho and referred to by Sextus as the "prophet of Pyrrho," was a contemporary of Arcesilaus. His refusal to join the Academy and his writings indicate that he did not view the skepticism of the Academy as identical to Pyrrhonism.

Hans Melzian, a scholar, has contributed significantly to the understanding of the Bini language, which is predominantly spoken in Southern Nigeria. His work, "A Concise Dictionary of the Bini Language," is a valuable resource for those interested in this linguistic field. The dictionary is available for free download, borrowing, and streaming through the Internet Archive. Alongside Melzian's contributions, another significant text on this topic is the autobiography of Jacob Egharevba, known as "ITAN ẸDAGBỌN MWEN." This autobiography is written in the Edo language, which is also one of the major languages spoken in Nigeria. The Edo language is spoken by the Edo people, who primarily reside in the Edo State of Nigeria. Both works offer significant insights into the languages and cultures of Southern Nigeria, enabling readers to gain a greater appreciation of the region's linguistic diversity. The availability of these resources online allows for a wider audience to access and appreciate the rich linguistic heritage of Nigeria.

The article examines the debate around the passing of Seth Rich, a member of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), and the way the media handled the coverage of the incident. Rod Wheeler, a private investigator, was hired by Rodger Stone and a wealthy Trump supporter, Ed Butowsky, to investigate Rich's murder. There were assertions that Rich had disclosed DNC emails to WikiLeaks, but these accusations have mostly been refuted. In May 2017, Fox News published a story suggesting a link between Rich and the FBI, which was later retracted. The report depended on Wheeler's findings, but he later claimed that the quotes attributed to him were fabricated. Wheeler filed a legal complaint against Fox News, alleging that the network had modified his statements in a defamatory manner. The lawsuit was dismissed in August 2018, with the judge ruling that there was no evidence of manipulation. Butowsky also faced a lawsuit from the Rich family, who accused him of exploiting their son's death for political purposes. The lawsuit was dismissed for similar reasons as Wheeler's, with the judge finding no evidence of wrongdoing on Butowsky's part. It is important to note that the claims of a connection between Rich, the DNC, and WikiLeaks have been widely discredited by multiple investigations, including those conducted by the U.S. intelligence community. The consensus among experts is that Russia was responsible for the hacking of the DNC's computer systems and the subsequent release of emails. In conclusion, the Seth Rich story has been a source of much controversy and misinformation. While some individuals have sought to use the incident to advance their political agendas, the evidence overwhelmingly points to Russia as the culprit behind the DNC hacking. It is crucial for the public to closely evaluate the information presented by the media and to rely on trustworthy sources for accurate reporting.

Suppose a President were elected on the promise of expanding military forces immediately following a European war. To delve deeper into these possible outcomes would be a slap in the face of our intelligence. The creation of so-called "defensive" alliances, whether directed against or in support of us—should we even be able to convince others to participate—would result in increasing hostility, acts of provocation, and a reliving of previous historical confrontations. However, should such a disastrous war ever take place, it would not be a tragedy if we had brought it upon ourselves. The real tragedy would be if we lacked the intrinsic value that Germany possesses to justify our actions. The deepest regret would be if we were so consumed by the failings of others that we failed to confront our own deficiencies. I Am Woman Marguerite Swawite I am woman: as ancient as the cedars of Lebanon and older still; as fresh as the youngest sprout pushing through the snow in March. My face is directed toward the East, glowing with the light of my emerging potential; my hands are held back by the restrictive embrace of the lone woman who, fueled by longing, sought only a kiss upon her neck and a child nestled in the bend of her arm. Today, I stand as a woman, a bit less yet a bit more; for I am learning to sing not his tune, nor anyone else's, but my own, which has dwelled within my heart since the very first day. It will be a grand golden song, though not always gentle with sweet cadence, for I must labor to sing. I am learning to live with emptiness, yet still discover satisfaction; to warm my frozen hands without fire; to continue moving ahead without a kiss or a child, even as my lips remain red and my arms stay prepared. Yet, I know I will never cease until I have sung it all—every last note. Even in the far-off days ahead, as they call to me at the break of dawn, I shall remain a woman. My song will become sweetly familiar, and he who was once frightened will draw near, singing his separate song, always his own, yet blending its masculine tones with mine. Together, we shall forge a remarkable harmony that embraces the world through our melodies, once again celebrating the joy of our union. That day will come... But today, I am weary—the East is rosy with the promise of dawn. (The following is one of the poems in Edgar Lee Master’s “Spoon River Anthology” which has been featured in Reedy’s St. Louis Mirror and has garnered widespread attention. In our view, it ranks as one of the most outstanding works of poetry. Caroline Branson With our hearts like drifting suns, had we only walked as often before the April fields until starlight softened the darkness under the rock, our trysting place in the wood, where the brook turns! Had we only transitioned from courtship like notes of music that merge, into the inspired improvisation of love! But to leave behind the enchantment of the flesh, in which our souls swooned, descending into a realm where time, space, and our individual selves ceased to exist—annihilated in love! To abandon these experiences for a room with lamps; to stand with our secret mocking itself, hiding among flowers and mandolins, observed by all between salad and coffee. To witness his trembling and feel my own premonition, as if signing a bond—not ablaze with gifts and pledges heaped with rosy hands over his brow. And then, O night! Deliberate! Unlovely! With all of our courtship erased by the act of love in a chosen room at an hour known to all. The next day, he sat so listless, almost cold, so strangely changed, wondering why I wept, until a kind of sick despair and voluptuous madness seized us, leading us to make the pact of death. A stalk of the earth sphere, fragile as starlight, awaits being drawn once again into creation's stream. But next time, to be born under the gaze of Raphael and St. Francis, as they pass by. For I am their younger sibling, to be clearly recognized face to face in a cycle of rebirth ahead. You may know the seed and the soil; you may feel the cold rain fall. But only the earth-sphere and heaven know the secret of the seed in the nuptial chamber under the soil. Throw me into the stream again, give me another trial—Save me, Shelley! Music The Kneisel Quartet and Hofmannized Chopin Albert Spalding What more fortunate combination could be desired than this: Albert Spalding performing the Mendelssohn Violin Concerto with the Thomas Orchestra! On two separate occasions, four thousand people felt genuine enthusiasm; and during both the Friday and Saturday concerts, the orchestra members (who usually maintain a calm demeanor as their typical reaction) were profoundly moved and showed the greatest degree of admiration for the young artist's talent. Frederick Stock beamed, fatherly, as he clapped his hands.

The Phoenician civilization, known for its maritime prowess and trade networks, has long been a subject of fascination and speculation regarding its influence on other cultures. One such debate revolves around the possibility of Phoenician contact with ancient American civilizations. However, the evidence supporting this theory is limited and often disputed. The Phoenicians are credited with developing an early form of the alphabet, which has influenced the writing systems used across Europe and Southwestern Asia today. This writing system is distinct from that employed by ancient American civilizations, such as those found at Palenque and Copan. The inscriptions in these American sites bear no resemblance to Phoenician writing, nor do they share any characteristics with the Phoenician language or architectural styles. In 1872, a stone purportedly inscribed with Phoenician script was discovered in Paraíba, Brazil. The inscription allegedly told the story of a Phoenician ship that was separated from a fleet sailing from Egypt around Africa during a storm. It also mentioned a pharaoh, either Necho I or Necho II. The stone was initially confirmed as genuine by Ladislau de Souza Mello Netto, who held the position of director at the National Museum of Brazil. However, by 1873, the philologist Ernest Renan had convinced Netto that the inscription was forged, as the forms of the letters were different from those used by the Phoenicians. The lack of a common language or writing system between the Phoenicians and ancient American groups, along with uncertainty about the true origin of the Paraíba stone, makes it difficult to establish a definitive connection between these two civilizations. While the idea of Phoenician influence on American civilizations is intriguing, the evidence currently available does not support this theory. Further research and discovery may shed more light on this topic in the future, but for now, the relationship between the Phoenicians and ancient American cultures remains speculative.

Mersenne, a well-known thinker and scholar from the 17th century, held the view that scientific investigation could establish principles and guidelines for understanding sensory experiences. He opposed the notion of doubting everything by emphasizing several key points: 1. Humans have common agreements on certain facts, such as the fact that an ant is smaller than an elephant. 2. Natural laws, including those related to optics, regulate our sensory experiences and assist in correcting errors. 3. Human-made instruments such as rulers and scales are employed to measure and remove uncertainty regarding occurrences like curved oars, pigeons' necks, and circular towers. However, a Pyrrhonist might counter these arguments by claiming that the senses can be misleading, leading to an unending cycle of doubt or circular reasoning. Mersenne countered this by arguing that widely accepted principles can be proposed and examined over time to confirm their accuracy. He also noted that if all things are subject to doubt, then the very act of doubting can itself be questioned, suggesting that a certain degree of certainty is essential. Mersenne maintained that mathematical, physical, and other scientific knowledge, having been subjected to thorough examination, is reliable and provides practical benefits. He was among the few philosophers who embraced Thomas Hobbes' bold ideas, viewing them as a fresh approach to understanding human behavior. Thomas Hobbes (1588-1679) was actively involved in the circle of major skeptics like Gassendi and Mersenne during his long stay in Paris. Although Hobbes shared an interest in skepticism and epistemology with his peers, he maintained a distinctive viewpoint that set him apart from them.

Renaissance Humanism emerged as a significant intellectual movement that flourished during the Renaissance period in Europe. It was marked by a revived focus on the exploration of classical antiquity, especially the literary works, philosophical ideas, and artistic achievements of ancient Greece and Rome. This movement sought to revive the values and knowledge of the ancient world and apply them to contemporary society. One of the main contributors to the rise of Renaissance Humanism was Lovato Lovato, an Italian poet and scholar. He was followed by other prominent humanists such as Leonardo Bruni, who further advanced the movement. The origins and evolution of humanism during this period have been extensively studied and documented by scholars like Ronald Witt in his work "In the Footsteps of the Ancients: The Origins of Humanism from Lovato to Bruni," published by Brill Publishers in 2000. Another important aspect of Renaissance Humanism was the influence of paganism. Edgar Wind, in his book "Pagan Mysteries in the Renaissance," published by W.W. Norton in 1969, explores the role of pagan beliefs and practices in shaping the cultural and intellectual landscape of the Renaissance. This book provides valuable insights into the complex relationship between Christianity and paganism during that period. Charles, in his work *The Scope of Renaissance Humanism*, published by the University of Michigan Press in 1983, presents an in-depth examination of the movement, its influence across different areas of society, and the significant individuals who played a role in shaping it. For those interested in learning more about Renaissance Humanism, there are several external resources available. The World History Encyclopedia provides an overview of the subject, while Albert Rabil Jr.'s "Humanism 1: An Outline" offers a concise introduction to the topic. Additionally, the Library of Congress's article "Rome Reborn: The Vatican Library & Renaissance Culture: Humanism," published on July 1, 2002, discusses the role of the Vatican Library in the preservation and dissemination of humanist ideas. Furthermore, the BBC Radio 4 program "In Our Time" featured a discussion on "Paganism in the Renaissance" with Tom Healy, Charles Hope, and Evelyn Welch on June 16, 2005. This conversation offers a compelling and enlightening view of how paganism shaped the Renaissance era. In summary, Renaissance Humanism was a crucial intellectual movement that sought to revive and apply the knowledge and values of classical antiquity to the contemporary world. The study of this movement offers a deeper understanding of the cultural and intellectual transformations that took place during the Renaissance.

The Ministry of Love in George Orwell's dystopian work "Nineteen Eighty-Four" plays an essential role. It is responsible for "rehabilitating" thought criminals, who are then released as loyal subjects brainwashed to adore Big Brother, thus embodying the Ministry's namesake. In various movie adaptations of the novel, the portrayal of Big Brother has differed across versions. In the 1954 BBC adaptation, production designer Roy Oxley was represented by a single still image. The 1956 movie version portrayed Big Brother as a severe, faceless head drawing. In the 1984 motion picture featuring John Hurt, the character of Big Brother was brought to life by actor Bob Flag. Both Oxley and Flag were shown with thin mustaches. Since the publication of "Nineteen Eighty-Four," the term 'Big Brother' has become widely used as a metaphor for any authority figure that is overly intrusive or controlling, as well as for government surveillance programs. The idea of Big Brother and other Orwellian symbols is frequently invoked in the comedic phrase referred to as the Russian reversal. In their 1956 work *Blood Royal*, Iain Moncreiffe and Don Pottinger humorously featured the line: "Without Little Father, there's no need for Big Brother," which alludes to the Russian Revolution and the Soviet Union. The global television series "Big Brother" draws its inspiration from the book's idea of ongoing monitoring. In 2000, after the premiere of the United States version of the CBS program "Big Brother," the Estate of George Orwell filed a lawsuit against CBS and its production company, Orwell Productions, Inc., in federal court in Chicago.

"Living by the Sword" is a phrase that has been used in various contexts to convey the idea that those who rely on violence or aggression typically suffer the repercussions of their actions. This concept can be traced back to historical and religious texts, suggesting that the use of force tends to perpetuate a cycle of violence. In mainstream culture, the phrase has appeared in songs. For instance, in Megadeth's song "Five Magics," frontman Dave Mustaine includes the line "He who lives by the sword, will surely also die," which echoes the sentiment of the proverb. In Bob Seger's song "Night Moves," the third verse features the phrase "Living by the Sword," showing how this expression remains influential in contemporary popular culture. The concept of living by the sword is often contrasted with the idea of Christian pacifism, which promotes nonviolence and peaceful conflict resolution. The phrase "turning swords into plowshares" is also closely related, as it symbolizes transforming weapons into tools for peaceful purposes, reflecting a shift from violence toward a more peaceful and cooperative society. While the phrase "living by the sword" has been used to discuss the consequences of a violent lifestyle, it is important to note that the interpretation and application of this concept can vary depending on the context in which it is used. As such, readers are encouraged to explore various perspectives and sources to form their own understanding of the phrase and its implications.

In the philosophical tradition of Scholasticism, the concept of the soul is central to understanding the nature of living beings. According to Thomas Aquinas and other Thomists, beings of the same genus share an essence, differing only in accidents and substantial form. The soul is defined as the substantial form of living beings, distinguishing them from one another. Plants possess what is known as "vegetative souls," which are responsible for their growth and development. Animals, on the other hand, are endowed with "sensitive souls," granting them the ability to perceive and react to their environment. Human beings are unique in that they possess "intellectual souls," which are characterized by rationality and immortality. Aristotle regarded the soul as a singular entity composed of five distinct capacities known as "dunámeis," which together form a unified whole. These faculties are: 1. The "vegetative" faculty (threptikón), which is concerned with the maintenance and development of organic life. 2. The inclination (oretikón), which refers to the tendency of seeking that which is regarded as beneficial. 3. The faculty of sense perception (aisthetikón), enabling the perception of the external world. 4. The "locomotive" faculty (kinetikón), which governs bodily movements. 5. Intellectual capacity (dianoetikón), considered the supreme faculty, is linked to reasoning and rational thinking. Scholastic philosophers generally follow Aristotle's classification, viewing the body and soul as a unified whole. The soul is considered the "forma substantialis," or the vital principle, that serves as the source of all activities. Therefore, examining the soul involves understanding processes that are commonly linked to biological and physiological fields today. The connection between the mind and the body falls under the domain of philosophical or metaphysical exploration. In relation to human desire, it may be divided into two parts: the rational and the irrational. The rational component is called the will, whereas the irrational part is termed passion. In the field of ethics, Thomas Aquinas supports Aristotle's concept of eudaimonia, describing it as "an action carried out entirely in line with virtue." He also claims that happiness is a condition that is exclusive to humans, as it is realized by practicing virtue. This perspective emphasizes the importance of moral and intellectual development in achieving a fulfilling and meaningful life.

"Very well, then," came the response, "but in exchange for my silence, you must inquire whether Kate has sewn the tassel on my smoking-cap as she promised." "Of course I did," a cheerful voice replied. Kate stepped out of the parlor, holding the cap in her hand, and looked even more beautiful than before. "Ah, thank you, dear Kate! Now do keep Paul in good spirits while I go to enjoy my cigar. It would be rude to leave him alone." Kate smiled, and their planned walk on the piazza was replaced with a stroll down the avenue. It must have been a delightful walk, for when the tea bell rang, they were still there, watching the pale moon rise, and wondering to themselves how often they would share such moments with the same pleasure. They didn't wonder for long. Each evening, Paul Linden would challenge someone to a walk, and somehow, everyone was tired except Kate, and everyone was busy except Kate. It didn't take long for the rustling leaves to catch sight of a promise of love between the two, and they would have heard (had they been able to listen) what Paul Linden considered the most soothing music on earth—the delicate tones that spoke to him of Kate de la Croix's tender heart. The leaves saw a strange ring gleaming on her fair hand, and they remained discreet—but not the sisters. Minnie noticed the small symbol representing their common faith, and sorrowful Kate revealed her secret to her while weeping and wailing. Even she was unhappy that night, as she recalled the outburst of grief that followed its revelation, and another bird left the nest almost as soon as the wedding was over. Mr. de la Croix smoked an unusually large amount of cigars that night as his daughter departed, and the sisters tried their best to remain hopeful; however, none of them were able to fall asleep without going into Kate's empty room to weep again. Lisa had to threaten to turn it into a storage room for rags before they could get used to passing by without entering and mourning her absence as if she would never return. "Don't keep crying over Kate," she would say; "she will be back, and you should wait until then to be happy." "But we miss her so much, Lisa," said Rose, her eyes full of tears. So do I, but you don't see me shedding tears over an old glove or a piece of writing like you do. And you can't say that I love her any less than the rest of her sisters." "Moreover, my dear girls," said Kenneth, taking his seat among them and lifting little Ernest onto his knee, "your spirits affect your father's. He feels the loss of his child, and you must all try to talk about her return, not her departure. I know how much you feel Kate's absence, but you must start looking at your separation as something that will happen one day. It is part of nature. There are three more people who will have to leave their homes; how could you possibly expect that everyone will be as lucky as Blanche and Kate, who stay with you just as they have done before? Paul's business will likely keep him away for a year, but he will return to settle here with us, and we must look at the bright side of things as long as we can. I have been telling all this to Blanche, who is just as calm and composed as Lisa; and now I come here to beg of you, for your own good, to face the unavoidable hardships with the bravery that becomes even more valuable once it has been earned. Minnie needs a scolding, I'm afraid," he continued, stroking her head affectionately. "Why don't you play the piano and sing as usual? The sound of music will lift our spirits, and the mechanical exercise of those little fingers will occupy your mind after a while, especially if you start working on those études by Moschelles, whose difficulty I have heard so much about." He smiled so encouragingly that Minnie hurried off to follow his advice, and soon after, Mr. de la Croix stepped out of his room, saying he was happy to hear the piano being played again. Minnie was fully rewarded when she saw him take his old seat and doze while she played; and she told Kenneth in confidence that she was grateful for the scolding, but he must not tell Lisa, because she might take advantage of it. That night, a long letter from Kate arrived, which helped to comfort them all. Poor Kate! Her return was supposed to be filled with sorrow, because during the journey, her beloved young daughter, her cherished Blanche, fell seriously ill and deteriorated so rapidly that by the time they got home, there was no hope of recovery left. Silently, they cradled her in their arms and carried her to her own room, laying the little sufferer on the bed.

At that time, Fra Giovanni Agnolo, who was later appointed a Cardinal by Pope Paul III, felt a deep sense of gratitude towards Angelo, the General at Arezzo. Angelo had looked after him and kindled in him a love for literature. In recognition of Angelo's influence, Agnolo crafted a stunning grey sandstone tomb for him in S. Piero, Arezzo. The tomb featured intricate carvings, a lifelike representation of General Angelo on the sarcophagus, and two life-size sculptures of weeping boys symbolizing the extinguishing of life's torch. Despite the tomb not being fully completed, Agnolo was summoned to Florence to assist with the city's festive preparations for the Emperor Charles V's victorious return from Tunis. Upon his arrival in Florence, Agnolo created an impressive eight-braccia figure of the River Arno on the Ponte a S. Trinita. The figure appeared to be rejoicing at the Emperor's arrival, along with other rivers depicted through statues made by different artists. Agnolo also created a twelve-braccia high figure of Jason, the leader of the Argonauts, on the Canto de' Carnesecchi. However, due to the large size and limited time, this work did not achieve the perfection of the Arno figure. Similarly, the figure of August Gladness he made on the Canto alla Cuculia did not meet the same acclaim. Although the timeframe was brief, Agnolo's creations garnered significant recognition and popularity among both artisans and the general public. After completing his work in Arezzo, Agnolo learned that Girolamo Genga had a marble project in Urbino. However, when the talks fell through, Agnolo made his way to Rome and subsequently to Naples, with the aim of constructing the tomb for the respected poet, Jacopo Sannazzaro. Sannazzaro had built a beautiful residence at Margoglino, which he bequeathed to the Order of Servite Friars upon his death. He instructed his executors, Signor Cesare Mormerio and the Lord Count d'Aliffe, to build his tomb in the church he had built. The friars proposed Agnolo for the task, and after receiving a significant portion of the payment, he commissioned Francesco del Tadda of Fiesole to assist with the project. While getting ready for the tomb's construction, Agnolo was approached by four prominent individuals who had been assigned the responsibility of strengthening Naples in preparation for the approaching Turkish forces. However, Agnolo, who considered it inappropriate for a religious person to engage in military endeavors, informed the executors that he would undertake the project either in Carrara or Florence. Agnolo then traveled to Florence, where he was commissioned by Signora Donna Maria, the mother of Duke Cosimo, to finish the S. Cosimo for the tomb of Lorenzo de' Medici. He also created a model for a Hercules statue to be placed atop a fountain at the Duke's villa at Castello. The model was well-received, and Agnolo was instructed to quarry the marble in Carrara. While in Carrara, Agnolo received a letter from Cardinal Doria, who sought a sculptor to complete a statue of Prince Doria, initially assigned to Bandinelli. Despite Cardinal Cibo's efforts to send Agnolo to Genoa, Agnolo insisted on fulfilling his commitment to Duke Cosimo first. During this time, he made significant progress on Sannazzaro's tomb and the Hercules statue. Upon returning to Florence, Agnolo worked diligently on the Hercules statue. However, rumors circulated that the marble was not as perfect as the model, and Agnolo faced difficulties fitting the legs to the torso. Messer Pier Francesco Riccio, the majordomo, began to withhold payments, influenced by Bandinelli's animosity towards Agnolo and the support of Tribolo, who was working on the Castello's ornaments. Feeling mistreated, Agnolo left for Genoa, where he received the commission for the statue of Prince Doria from Cardinal Doria and the Prince. He finished the statue while continuing to supervise the construction of Sannazzaro's tomb. The statue was well-received in Genoa, but Agnolo was disappointed when it was placed on the Piazza della Signoria instead of the Piazza Doria, as he had designed it to stand alone on a pedestal. In conclusion, the placement of a work of art is crucial to its visual impact, as the artist considers the lighting and viewing angles during its creation.

The Catholic University of Taiwan is well known for creating the initial graduate program in philosophy in that area. The institution's latest slogan, "Truth, Goodness, Beauty, Sanctity," reflects its dedication to promoting scholarly development and exploration in the realm of philosophy. This vision played a key role in establishing the Fu Jen Philosophy Department, which grew into a major hub for Scholasticism in Taiwan. The department's rise to prominence can be largely attributed to the impactful philosophical ideas of Yu Pin, especially his theory of the "Three Kinds of Knowing" (三知論). Over the six decades following World War II, the university's philosophical endeavors evolved into a unique school of thought, deeply rooted in the rich history of Christian philosophy. The collective work of scholars at Fu Jen Catholic University has been recognized as the "Chinese Neo Scholastic Philosophy" group. This intellectual movement has come to be known as the "Fu Jen School," reflecting the university's lasting influence in the realm of philosophy. Notable members of this group include Bernard Li, Gabriel Chen, Ying Ly, Chien-ming Chu, and Hsiao Chih Sun. The university's academic achievements are additionally highlighted by its publication, "Universitas: Monthly Review of Philosophy and Culture," which appears in the Arts & Humanities Citation Index (A&HCI). Fu Jen Religious Studies is another significant area of research within the institution. For further study of related subjects, one might consult the Kyoto School, a Japanese intellectual movement that exhibits certain philosophical parallels with the Fu Jen School. Further exploration and supplementary materials may offer a more comprehensive grasp of Scholasticism and the philosophical traditions that have influenced the scholarly environment at Fu Jen Catholic University.

In the 1980s, a significant rise in culturally and creatively progressive people occurred, introducing new concepts that helped shape the evolution of an alternative way of living. Larry Butler stood out as one of the leading members of this group of forward-thinking individuals. He worked as a custodian at the Diorama, the initial movie house in London, situated in Regent's Park. Butler was not only a dedicated caretaker but also a pioneer in the field of communication, known for his genius and innovative leadership. The Diorama building served as a central gathering place for artists and performers during the late 1970s. They developed an interdisciplinary method covering multiple areas such as art, education, counseling, and artistic programs for individuals with disabilities, as noted on the website My Camden. Between 1981 and 1992, the Diorama Arts Centre (DAC) underwent significant changes and challenges. In response to a request from the Crown Estate Commissioners (CEC), the Diorama Arts Centre became a registered charity and company on September 15, 1981. In 1982, a formal lease agreement was put in place, taking the place of the earlier minimal peppercorn rent of around £25 annually. In 1983, the group faced the threat of eviction as Greycoats Estates, acting on behalf of the CEC, planned to redevelop the Diorama into office spaces. However, the Diorama Arts Centre fought against this attempted eviction and emerged victorious in 1984 after a public inquiry conducted by the Department of the Environment. The victory was aided by the 'Re-use of Industrial Buildings Service' provided by URBED (Urbanism, Environment, and Design Ltd.). By February 1984, the Diorama Arts Trust came into existence with the aim of putting forward a plan that resulted in a £4 million fundraising campaign, which continued past the year 1984. CAST (Cartoon Archetypical Slogan Theatre), led by Roland Muldoon, also agreed to support the cause, further strengthening the movement.

The concept of desire and its relationship to will is a fascinating one. Desire might act as the basis for the development of will, and as time goes on, will can ultimately become independent and even surpass its original source. This is particularly evident in habitual actions, where individuals often continue to perform certain actions out of habit, even when the original motivation has faded. This phenomenon is not limited to virtuous actions but can also apply to neutral or even harmful behaviors that have become ingrained over time. The distinction between will and desire is an important psychological fact. Will, like all aspects of our nature, is susceptible to habituation. We could end up performing an action not due to our desire for it, but simply because we have become accustomed to it. This is the power of habit, which can influence our actions even when they contradict our conscious preferences. In the case of virtue, a weak will can be strengthened by cultivating a desire for it. By associating virtuous actions with pleasure and vice versa, we can evoke a will to be virtuous that, once established, operates independently of the original motivations of pleasure or pain. Will is born from desire but eventually comes under the influence of habit. Although the result of habit might not always be morally positive, the consistency it brings to our emotions and actions is essential for maintaining the dependability of our will to act rightly. The idea of utility, which claims that happiness or pleasure constitutes the highest form of good, is directly connected to this conversation. If we recognize that action is motivated by desire and habit, and that these are shaped by experiences of pleasure and pain, then the principle of utility becomes more plausible. However, the validity of this principle is left for the reader to consider. The connection between justice and utility is another complex issue. The strong sentiment associated with justice often leads people to view it as an absolute quality, distinct from the concept of expediency. Yet, the sense of justice, much like other innate tendencies, might need direction from a higher form of reasoning to guarantee its correct use. The origin of the feeling of justice does not necessarily legitimize all its promptings. Even if justice is an instinct, it may still need to be controlled and enlightened by reason. The personal sense of justice might differ from that of mere convenience, yet this does not imply that justice cannot be regarded as a component of overall benefit. To grasp the essence of justice, one must consider whether the perception of justice and injustice is distinct or originates from other emotions. If the feeling of justice is found to be a combination of other feelings, it may be possible to explain its intensity and character through the general laws of our emotional constitution. When looking for shared qualities between just and unjust behaviors, it is important to examine a range of instances. One common perception is that it is unjust to deprive someone of their personal liberty, property, or anything else that belongs to them by law. This view, along with several others, will be examined in greater detail to identify the key characteristics that distinguish justice from injustice.

The French cavalry was famous for its skill, covering an extensive area of fifteen square miles. Each cavalry unit comprised a total of one hundred and twenty horses, mostly the half-bred Percheron type, with black and grey being the most frequent coat colors. A fierce sense of competition existed between the companies, all working hard to keep their teams in peak physical condition. These teams were often depicted in paintings, showcasing the men engaged in various tasks such as chopping and sawing down trees. John Nash, a well-known British painter, placed great emphasis on the significance of an artist's visual sharpness and fine motor skills. He believed that an artist's primary task is to train their eye to observe, probe, and then synchronize their hand movements with their visual perception. Nash's most renowned war artwork, "Over the Top," is an oil painting on canvas that measures 79.4 by 107.3 centimeters and is now on display at the Imperial War Museum in London. This painting captures the 30th December 1917 Welsh Ridge counter-attack, during which the 1st Battalion Artists Rifles (28th London Regiment) advanced from their trenches towards Marcoing, close to Cambrai. Tragically, out of the eighty men involved, sixty-eight were either killed or injured within the first few minutes of the attack. Nash himself was among the twelve who succeeded in surviving the fierce machine gun fire depicted in the artwork. He completed this powerful piece three months after the event. "Over the Top" offers a vivid and compelling depiction of soldiers charging into combat, clearly acknowledging the serious danger of not surviving the ordeal. Nash's depiction conveys the raw emotion and harsh reality of war, as he recounts the experience of soldiers falling to the ground, some with screams and others in silence, as their comrades continue to push forward.

Examen philosophicum, originating from Latin as "philosophic exam" and commonly shortened to Ex.phil., serves as one of the two main academic assessments in most undergraduate courses at Norwegian universities. It is supported by the Examen facultatum, which is aimed at teaching students how to master the skills of academic writing. In contrast, the Examen philosophicum aims to enhance students' understanding of philosophical ideas and their ability to think in an organized manner. The Examen philosophicum originated when it was first introduced at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark-Norway in 1675. However, it was discontinued in Denmark in 1971, and its presence in Norway has since been reduced. The required status of Examen philosophicum as a subject is formally recognized by royal decrees specific to each institution. For instance, the Regulations of 20 December 2005 No. 1798 on Studies and Exams at the University of Oslo serve as a legal basis for its implementation. Both the Examen philosophicum and Examen facultatum are essential parts of most bachelor's degree programs in Norway. Exceptions to this general rule are primarily found in professional programs at university colleges and a few natural science disciplines at universities, where taking one or both examinations may be exempted. The curriculum of the Examen philosophicum can differ between universities and fields of study, usually adapted to match the academic emphasis of each department and the specific area of focus within the undergraduate program. For example, students pursuing a major in foreign languages will participate in a course of study that has been specially designed to fit their particular field of concentration. Generally, the Examen philosophicum encompasses the study of philosophy, ethics, and rhetoric. The University of Oslo continued the tradition of Examen philosophicum by introducing it in 1812, just two years after the university was established. This academic examination continues to play a significant role within the Norwegian higher education system, fostering students' ability to think critically and gain a more profound understanding of philosophical concepts.

As they journeyed through the lush countryside of Hertfordshire and the verdant expanses of the Warwickshire coach roads, the man of the cloth noticed a subtle change in his companion, George Stobart. Despite the picturesque vistas and the warm embrace of the sun, Stobart seemed preoccupied, his gaze distant, his thoughts elsewhere. The seasoned traveler, known for his punctuality and politeness, was also renowned for his wide sympathies. He had quickly assessed Stobart's character and found it to be of true mettle. Yet, he could not help but express his concern about the young man's apparent distraction. "I hope you do not begin to tire of your work, Stobart," he said, his voice filled with genuine concern. "I have seen many young men start with fervor, only to lose their way when faith wavers. But I do not believe you are one of them. However, I sense that something troubles you." "I am troubled, sir," Stobart admitted, his voice heavy with worry. "I am troubled by a soul I am trying to win for Christ, but with little success." The experienced man, possessing sharp perception, deduced the origin of Stobart's worry. "It is about your cousin's widow, Lady Kilrush, is it not?" he asked, his gaze piercing. "You have told me of her generous nature and her unconventional beliefs. I understand your desire to bring her into the fold, out of gratitude for her support of your work among the poor." Stobart was taken aback by the man's intuition. "Indeed, sir, you have guessed correctly. I have attempted to talk sense into her, but her fierce temper and her condescending attitude make it challenging. It seems that the forces of darkness have the upper hand, and it is easier to deny than to prove. When I am with her, I find myself forgetting the spiritual danger she is in, even as she saves others from physical suffering." The wise man chided Stobart gently. "You have focused too much on the woman and not enough on her soul. Her beauty has clouded your judgment. As your mentor and friend, I caution you against placing too much value on the companionship of a beautiful heathen, unless your only purpose is her redemption. Stobart was quick to defend himself. "I assure you, sir, I have never entertained an unworthy thought about Lady Kilrush. She has always treated me with sisterly affection. Her beauty does not alter my concern for her soul. I would give half my life to save her from the dangers of worldly pleasures and the company of the unscrupulous." "If you can keep your conscience clear and win this woman from the clutches of Satan, you will have done well," the wise man advised. "But do not compromise the truth. If you fail to guide her towards righteousness, you must part ways with her forever." The conversation took a personal turn as the wise man shared his own experiences. "You know, Stobart, I too have known the pain of unrequited love. The woman I loved before Mrs. Wesley was a domestic worker, but her intelligence and demeanor were deserving of the greatest respect. Circumstances prevented our union, and I made another choice." His voice trailed off with a sigh, revealing the depth of his unspoken sorrow. Stobart spent a month on the road with his mentor, preaching in Bristol and to the miners of Kingswood. They traveled from south to north, accompanied by one of Wesley's earliest and most gifted lay preachers. This humble man, despite his lowly birth, was a powerful orator, capable of stirring the hearts of those who had never heard the Word of God. The journey was filled with hardships and inconveniences, but the travelers bore them with good humor, inspired by Wesley's cheerful spirit and Christian contentment. By the time they arrived in London during May, Stobart had already spent more than a month away from home. He had received weekly letters from his wife, detailing her household concerns and their child's growth. He, in turn, wrote to her about his adventures, knowing she took great interest in the fine houses he visited and the social customs he observed. Their bond, while lacking the early fervor of passionate love, was marked by consistent affection and reciprocal respect. Stobart thought he had made a wise choice in marrying the printer's daughter, for she gave him the liberty to follow his spiritual path. During the religious pilgrimage, Stobart had written several letters to Lady Kilrush, inspired by his conversations with Wesley and his spiritual experiences.
